body: I think `TextCluster` could be a dictionary, instead of a non-constructible but mutable class. Do you agree, or is there something I'm missing?

The `TextCluster` object must also store internally the context's styles like `font` and I guess all of the `CanvasTextDrawingStyles`, as they were when `measureText()` has been called, so I suppose an interface makes sense?  

However it's unclear why it's mutable indeed, nor why the `text` is exposed and not just stored internally too. IIUC, it's the original text that was passed to `measureText`, so I suppose authors should already know it.  

Also the `x` and `y` arguments to `fillTextCluster()` are a bit unclear to me. I guess they're the equivalent of `fillText`'s `x` and `y`, but in that case how come they can be optional?

It seems this intends to cover some of the same use cases as #10650.

cc @whatwg/canvas @khushalsagar

> I think `TextCluster` could be a dictionary, instead of a non-constructible but mutable class. Do you agree, or is there something I'm missing?

You're right. We originally thought of as a interface since the underlying object has to save references to other objects and it felt more natural, but having it be a dictionary is more useful from the user's side. Plus, a standard dictionary would allow to create modified copies via the spread syntax. I'll update it.

> The `TextCluster` object must also store internally the context's styles like `font` and I guess all of the `CanvasTextDrawingStyles`, as they were when `measureText()` has been called, so I suppose an interface makes sense?

Indeed, that is the idea. In the current prototype in Chromium (CL is currently under review), the `TextCluster` object holds a reference to the font in order to replicate the text accurately even if the font set in the context has changed (which is also relevant if the font wasn't fully loaded when `measureText()` was called). We had originally thought of only the font but I agree that it's better to include all `CanvasTextDrawingStyles`.

> However it's unclear why it's mutable indeed, nor why the `text` is exposed and not just stored internally too. IIUC, it's the original text that was passed to `measureText`, so I suppose authors should already know it.

We think it can be useful to allow the creation of `TextClusters` directly from JS if desired. In that case it would be the author's responsibility to guarantee that no ligatures or glyphs are separated. For that to work the whole text is needed as context to enable the correct shaping of the ligatures or other context-dependent modifications that the font can define. For all other attributes, I agree that we should make them immutable. I will update that too.

> Also the `x` and `y` arguments to `fillTextCluster()` are a bit unclear to me. I guess they're the equivalent of `fillText`'s `x` and `y`, but in that case how come they can be optional?

The idea for the `x` and `y` arguments passed to `fillTextCluster()` is that by rendering all the clusters returned by `getTextClusters()` at a specific position, the rendered result is exactly the same as calling `fillText()` at that same position. In other words, it works as a delta for the internal `x` and `y` attributes that are part of the `TextCluster` object. If they are not passed, the values from `TextCluster` are used directly (so the equivalent call would be `ctx.fillText(text, 0, 0)`).

Thanks for your comments!

> We think it can be useful to allow the creation of `TextClusters` directly from JS if desired. 

I fail to see how this could work. As per your previous point, authors would also need to define all of the `CanvasTextDrawingStyles` inside that object for the engine to make sense of it. You'll then enter the issue of how an author can point to an actual font. As a string? Then when is it parsed? It could be as a `FontFace` but that would be quite novel since the 2D context doesn't accept this kind of object yet. 
I might have missed it in the explainer, but I guess it would be clearer to me if you could share an example use-case for the ability to modify a `TextCluster`, or to create one from scratch without going through `measureText().getTextClusters()`.  

> (so the equivalent call would be `ctx.fillText(text, 0, 0)` ).

I think that'd be the first such positioning argument that defaults to `0` in the whole API. That feels odd to me.
Sorry, I'm a bit confused. Dictionaries can't save references to other objects, so if that's indeed needed, then staying with the current interface design makes the most sense.

> It seems this intends to cover some of the same use cases as #10650.
> 
> cc @whatwg/canvas @khushalsagar

Yes, the issues are related in that they came out of the same discussions and prior proposals for improving canvas text. The editing aspects of this proposal could be covered by just inserting HTML content and editing that, but the proposal here is simpler from both an implementation and author perspective.

The access to text cluster information is unique to this proposal and really to a canvas context where the author has direct control of placement of everything.

> I fail to see how this could work. As per your previous point, authors would also need to define all of the `CanvasTextDrawingStyles` inside that object for the engine to make sense of it. You'll then enter the issue of how an author can point to an actual font. As a string? Then when is it parsed? It could be as a `FontFace` but that would be quite novel since the 2D context doesn't accept this kind of object yet. I might have missed it in the explainer, but I guess it would be clearer to me if you could share an example use-case for the ability to modify a `TextCluster`, or to create one from scratch without going through `measureText().getTextClusters()`.

For modification, the main use case we have thought of so far would be to actually draw the cluster at the position `x, y` passed to `fillTextCluster()`. This is useful if you want to animate your text as a rotating circle. It's possible to use the `x` value from each cluster as a way to know where in the circle that cluster should start. But after that, it would be better to be able to call `fillTextCluster()` with the actual final position for the cluster, and that requires making the `x` and `y` values stored in cluster `0`.  Allowing the modification of these two values is (at least for now) our approach for this use case. The rest of the attributes of `TextCluster` should be immutable though, I agree. 

For the manual creation of `TextCluster` objects, we thought of it as a potentially interesting feature but if it feels not useful or inconsistent I'm okay with not allowing authors to do that directly, and only supporting clusters originating from `getTextClusters()`. Our original idea in that case was to use the `CanvasTextDrawingStyles` from the rendering context if they aren't available from the `TextCluster`, but now I realize that can even have inconsistencies with changes in the context state. So I agree on that too!

> > (so the equivalent call would be `ctx.fillText(text, 0, 0)` ).
> 
> I think that'd be the first such positioning argument that defaults to `0` in the whole API. That feels odd to me.

After discussing I realized I mixed this with another default. This default is just a remanent of how my first prototype was implemented. I agree the `x` and `y` in `fillTextCluster()` shouldn't be optional. I will update the explainer accordingly.

What does `TextCluster` really represent?
Is `TextMetrics` the right place to clusterize the text? `TextMetrics` is just metrics for a string. Making `TextMetrics.getTextClusters()` return `sequence<TextCluster>` where each `TextCluster` has `DOMString` is strange. `TextMetrics` does not return the string it measures. It does not know the `x` and `y` this string will be displayed at. But the returned `TextCluster` knows its `x` and `y`. 

I think what you are trying to do is a job of `TextAnalyzer`, `TextItemizer` or `TextClusterizer` more than a job of `TextMetrics`.

The name of this method is a little bit confusing:
```
unsigned long caretPositionFromPoint(double offset);
```
First it does not return a `CaretPosition`.  It just returns an offset in a string. Second it does not take a point like `Document.caretPositionFromPoint()`. It just takes a distance from the origin of display.

> The name of this method is a little bit confusing:
> 
> ```
> unsigned long caretPositionFromPoint(double offset);
> ```
> 
> First it does not return a `CaretPosition`. It just returns an offset in a string. Second it does not take a point like `Document.caretPositionFromPoint()`. It just takes a distance from the origin of display.

Yes, I agree there is some potential for confusion in the arguments differing from the DOM version, but there is some discoverability benefit to having the same name. Would `caretLocationFromOffset()` be an improvement?

Post WHATWG meeting action items:
* Rename caretPositionFromPoint to caretLocationFromOffset.
* Should we provide a locale to get consistent rendering of text in a logo, overwriting the local settings to get a consistent rendering (for company logos, for instance). Look at the SVG solution to this kind of thing.
* Examine the relationship to Intl.Segmenter.

I think `caretLocationFromOffset` is still a bit weird. There's no caret here. And we don't call a string index a location. It's also unclear whether this accounts for grapheme clusters or not. And if it does, perhaps locale needs to be an input here or elsewhere? `indexFromOffset()` or some such seems more closely aligned with JavaScript.
cc @whatwg/i18n

> I think `caretLocationFromOffset` is still a bit weird. There's no caret here. And we don't call a string index a location. It's also unclear whether this accounts for grapheme clusters or not. And if it does, perhaps locale needs to be an input here or elsewhere? `indexFromOffset()` or some such seems more closely aligned with JavaScript.

"index" is exactly what I was thinking after the meeting yesterday.

The behavior here accounts for graphemes the same way that document.caretLocationFromPoint does (generally we use the same underlying code, though not quite in the Chromium case). It's also the code that decides the boundaries of a selection range. It tries to split ligatures but gives the first or last index of a grapheme cluster depending on the bidi direction and whether this point is the start or end of the selection range. For a single point query we take the start of the cluster in the bidi direction.

Don't even get me started on figuring out an index from point in a mixed bidi string. The best logic there is highly context dependent and there is no existing spec language to cover it, nor do I think there should be.

Regarding compatibility with the TC399 [`Intl.Segmenter`](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#segmenter-objects) function and associated data.

It definitely seems worth considering the use of JS for segmentation and change the `getTextClusters` to take a `Segments` instance, returning x,y,width,height for each segment. The major advantage of this is "free" support for localisation control plus options to control how segmentation occurs. e.g. we could get per-word or per-line segmentation. I can see some value to that. The downside is that the JS segmentation may be the same as the layout/rendering segmentation, making it more complex to convert the indexes to rects, particularly given localisation.

The biggest challenge to this proposal is that the `Segment` objects in JS exist only in JS; they are not objects created from idl bindings. We manage to handle this for `Date` and `String` so it should be possible in theory. Practice is another matter.

I've compared the results of the [Intl.Segmenter](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#segmenter-objects) `segment` function and Chromium's implementation of `TextMetrics.getTextClusters` and they differ in a key respect. The JS method clusters but does not perform visual re-ordering for BIDI, whereas for the canvas case we want the clusters in visual order.

We could have `TextMetrics.getTextClusters` take a [Segments instance](https://tc39.es/ecma402/#sec-segments-objects) and then map it into visual order and compute geometric information. The advantage of that is localization info is present in the clustering. The canvas implementation would need to compute visual order runs and then map the grapheme indices onto those runs, then shape each grapheme for geometric information.

It doesn't seem worth it right now.
The `lang` attribute doesn't work for `OffscreenCanvas` though. And if it's an actual input we should make that explicit.

> The options to getTextClusters give parameters to use when computing the cluster positions. The same options to fillTextCluster override the values used when the set of clusters was generated with getTextClusters.
> 
> There is an example using these options to render text on a circle.

A bit more context on the options parameter for `fillTextCluster()`:

This came about as an answer to concerns expressed here about why weren't all the attributes of a `TextCluster` object `readonly`. Our reasoning for keeping the `x` and `y` attributes mutable before was enabling cases like in the example above, in which the positional data of the clusters is used to make some calculation (in this case, where on the circle to place each cluster based on its `x` value compared to the whole width), but then render the cluster at a specific location based on that calculation.

We agree that it's better to have all attributes as `readonly`, so we came up with this options parameter for `fillTextCluster()` that can override these values, as well as the `align` and `baseline`, that are used to render the cluster to provide this flexibility without having to modify the cluster at all. This way, the options for selecting what position is desired when measuring the text and obtaining the cluster can be independent of the options used to render if desired. 

Please let us know what you think!

> The `lang` attribute doesn't work for `OffscreenCanvas` though. And if it's an actual input we should make that explicit.

Offscreen canvas should be fixed to accept lang, because it also renders text and one would not expect the offscreen canvas font choices to differ from the canvas you are putting the offscreen content into. That would be adding an optional locale to the constructor for OffscreenCanvas. If the offscreen is created from a canvas element it would get the canvas element's locale.

I suppose that's a separate issue.
Created https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/10862 for adding a `lang` parameter for offscreen canvas. Right now it always users the OS locale, it seems.

I still have a problem with this proposal for two reasons:

1. You are adding to a `TextAnalyzer` to `TextMetrics` which is tied to the selected font. `TextClusters` are more than just splitting the text. I think it deserves its own new interface.
2. Analyzing text and using the output of this analysis has to go through multiple steps not just calling TextMetrics.getTextClusters(). Theses steps are:
- **Analysis**: Text will be split to something like `TextGroup`. All characters in a `TextGroup` have the same language and the same bi-directional level. This step does not need any font. It just depends on the code points of the text.
- **Shaping**: each `TextGroup` can be shaped in one step using the current selected font. The result of this step are (1) a set of `TextClusters`, (2) glyph points in the font and (3) positions for the glyphs. One glyph can map to one or more one character for example multiple Arabic characters can be displayed by one glyph. And in some Indic languages a character can be displayed by more than one glyph. A `TextCluster` is the smallest displayable unit of `TextGroup`. It maps one or more characters from the `TextGroup` to one or more glyphs. For example a `TextCluster` can map one character to multiple glyphs or map multiple characters to one glyph. Shaping also returns the glyph positions assuming the text is displayed horizontally at x = 0. In this step also, the font substitution will also be applied. For example a TextCluster may be split because not all the glyphs in it can be displayed by the selected font. And a font substitute has to be used instead. 
- **Justification**: This step is optional step where glyph positions are shifted to expand or shrink to a certain width. In Arabic, the glyphs will be expanded by Kashidas. In other languages, inter character and inter word justification can be applied by spaces.
- **Usage**: In this case,`TextGroups` can be displayed, measured or hit-tested. A web developer should not have to loop through `TextClusters`, glyphs or characters to map from a display offset to a character index.

To summarize if you want to add the text analysis to the canvas, please choose where the interface should be carefully and do it in full. Text analysis is a complex subject. It is more than just splitting and measuring the text.

I hear the concerns about the text analysis implied by this proposal. As is current;y proposed there is an implicit step to convert to `TextGroup` aka text runs, then each is shaped, then the shaping results are exposed. And all of those steps are non-trivial and not even consistently done between browsers in some cases. But what is the alternative for achieving the desired enhancements for authors?

In particular, `TextGroups` as proposed are a different level of granularity that in most cases would be exactly the same as the input string. Mixed bidi runs are not common. So making `TextGroups` the unit for display etc does not add anything most of the time.

To achieve per-glyph positioning and shading it is necessary to provide per-glyph data in some form. There are other ways to go about this such as text-on-path and some form of styling per-glyph, but they are less general than this proposal. Is that what you would propose to address the use cases?

Regarding things like `indexFromPosition`, these are based on existing DOM APIs that already handle all the bidi re-ordering and shaping implicitly. It's even possible to write JS to produce the same output as `getTextClusters()` does, though with a lot more script and computation. That is, use DOM APIs for `offsetFromPoint` to search for the position transition points, then use the substrings implied by that analysis as the text clusters. This proposal is exposing the same thing without all the JS.

In preparation for the upcoming session at the WebeEnginesHackfest, I thought I'll share a proposal that Ian Roth and I wrote at Google in 2012 towards similar goals: 

https://docs.google.com/document/d/151ZZAJVo2nysvBVAAjW_9cK02T5vWHy2sClNl2eXnsA/edit

Thanks to those who attended the session on this topic at the Web Engines Hackfest. This summarizes the primary discussion points:

1. The `getTextClusters` method doesn't seem to fit with the `TextMetrics` object produced by `measureText`. The only way they relate right now is an implementation detail, in that both can rely on the decomposition of the test string into bidi runs. But that's not a great reason.
2. There is missing functionality to support text strings with mixed bidi text and multiple fonts or other text styles required for the run, yet a desire to have the run be shaped as a unit. Note that HTML doesn't support this but we view canvas as a low level API to get precise control over text rendering, so providing such functionality is worthwhile.
3. HTML-in-Canvas is likely to be the preferred approach for editing text in canvas when the text is laid out in a "typical" way. But if you are breaking text into clusters and drawing them on a path, you would want some kind of editing support for the decomposed text.

There were some pointers to other proposals too that I still need to follow up on. [Here are the raw notes](https://hackmd.io/lGXMlKhlSPWfNF6IAn0YTA).

We have a proposal for addressing the concerns raised.

Specifically:
* Move the `getTextClusters` method out of `TextMetrics` and into a new mixin, maybe `CanvasTextClusters`. Addresses 1.
* Add cluster bounding box information to the `TextCluster` object. The editing functionality, particularly the ability to select text, is most useful when text is broken into clusters and rendered on a complex path, so put the bound information there. Addresses 3.
* Remove the bounding box and caret-from-offset additions from TextMetrics because for standard text layout their functionality is covered by HTML-in-Canvas. Addresses 3.
* For the future, consider a `SegmentedText` object that encapsulates a text run broken into segments with per-segment `CanvasTextStyles`, bidi information and the like. Add a version of `measureText` and `getTextClusters` that take a `SegmentedText` object and generate metrics and clusters for the entire run taking into account the segment properties. Addresses 2 in the future. We believe this would be an addition that the current proposal does not preclude, and we would like to get agreement on the other portions while continuing to work on this idea.

I'd like to talk about this more at the next WHATNOT meeting in the AMER-EMEA timeslot (that's July 16, I believe). Please let us know your thoughts on the issue here.

I thought I had replied to Anne's comment but apparently not. I just meant that the smallest unit of text styling available to authors in HTML is the <span>. Browsers do indeed automatically choose fonts to reasonably render the given text and can handle multiple fonts within a single <span>.

One issue that has been raised with the new proposal is the efficiency of splitting CanvasTextClusters out of TextMetrics because they share the underlying need to shape a text run, which is somewhat expensive. One option is to introduce an intermediate `ShapedText`  opaque object constructed from a string and text styles, and provide it for both `measureText` and `getTextClusters`.
Note I already added the issue to the meeting notes doc.

Thanks for putting this summary together. We've gone over the notes and see some solid common ground, but we also have concerns about deprecating the existing metrics.
1. Structural changes (Phase 1) Moving getTextClusters to a CanvasTextClusters mixin makes sense. Adding bounding box properties directly to TextCluster is also a good idea that we can support right away, as it helps with use cases like drawing text on a path.
2. SegmentedText (Phase 2) We should bump the SegmentedText proposal to a Phase 2 track. Pulling complex localization tasks (like bidi resolution and multi-font shaping) into Canvas steps outside its usual low-level scope. Custom layout engines generally just want raw browser metrics to feed into their own logic.
3. Keeping range metrics We need to keep getActualBoundingBox for text ranges. You can't just add up the bounding boxes of individual clusters to get the exact bounds of a phrase—kerning, ligatures, and italic overlaps throw the math off. Keeping range metrics (alongside getSelectionRects) gives developers an accurate invalidation rect without forcing them to write complex workarounds.
4. HTML-in-Canvas timeline HTML-in-Canvas looks promising, but it's still in the early draft stages. Dropping working metrics like getIndexFromOffset and range bounds now because a future standard might handle them would leave current frameworks stranded.
Proposed action plan: To keep the API moving forward without breaking things for current consumers, we suggest splitting this into two distinct phases.
Phase 1 (Immediate updates):
Refactor the interface to introduce the CanvasTextClusters mixin.
Expand TextCluster to include cluster-specific bounding boxes to unblock the text-on-a-path scenarios.
Keep getActualBoundingBox, getIndexFromOffset, and getSelectionRects on TextMetrics intact so current custom layout engines don't lose critical range data.
Phase 2 (Exploration):
Spin off the SegmentedText concept into a separate thread.
Use that space to figure out how Canvas should properly interact with complex bidi algorithms and multi-font inputs without bloating the core API.

I recently discovered this proposal when speaking with Thomas Nettestad at three.js conf in paris.
I am maintaining a rust based font shaping/rendering library `@pmndrs/glyph` targeting WebGL and WebGPU, and have been working with Skia/CanvasKit in open source projects. 

Typically font rendering in WebGL/WebGPU is achieved by baking a texture or buffer atlas per glyph from the font outlines ahead of time, for instance the MSDF rendering technique uses an SDF based glyph atlas, while Slug uses an analytic buffer indexed by glyph to describe the outlines as quadratics.

If this API were to also emit a font local glyph id for the font face it would be trivial to lookup a glyph in an atlas and derive all the shaping from this new API, enabling high performance font rendering and shaping in a 3D accelerated canvas. For multi-glyph clusters, I would prefer something like the following data available for each glyph in addition to the current API.

```ts
interface ShapedGlyph {
  glyphId: number // Font-local glyph index, equivalent to shaped hb_glyph_info_t.codepoint.
  cluster: number // UTF-16 input offset, matching the surrounding Canvas text API.
  xAdvance: number // CSS px in the text run's local coordinate system.
  yAdvance: number // CSS px in the text run's local coordinate system.
  xOffset: number // CSS px from the run pen position.
  yOffset: number // CSS px from the run pen position.
}
```

This could potentially be collapsed to local offsets based on the current start position of the multi-glyph cluster, or presented in some other way that would allow recomputing the glyph that is being selected in the font from the source UTF-16 code point. For this particular use case the pixels in the canvas that render the final font are of minimal value, as the cononical rendering technique being selected has already computed optimized outlines into textures and buffers being copied to the GPU.

If it is of any interest, here is my current plan for [implementing this API](https://github.com/pmndrs/glyph/issues/176) outlining drawbacks and variable approaches against the full wasm library built on HarfRust that essentially re-implements most of the core font shaping being done in the browser already.

The WebKit proposal is [here](https://github.com/WebKit/explainers/pull/137), and you'll see related WHATWG issues linked just above this comment. In the coming days I will reconcile the proposals and write up my conclusions.

Hi! I maintain [Pretext](https://github.com/chenglou/pretext), a small library that works out how a browser will break a paragraph into lines without touching the DOM, so an app can size and virtualize thousands of text blocks with no layout pass. All it asks the browser is `measureText()` on an OffscreenCanvas. I'm working on a speculative revamp of it that tries to match each browser's own lines exactly, and I wanted to share what `getTextClusters()` did for that, since it turned out to be a much bigger deal than I expected. Thanks for building it.

Some background on why. Blink shapes a whole run once and breaks lines inside the shaped result, so to break where Blink breaks I need to know where each glyph cluster sits inside the run, and `measureText()` gives me a total. So I measure prefix after prefix, then small windows around each offset to work out which glyph a kern landed on, then the same windows with ligatures off. For an ordinary chat message (about 110 characters, 16px Helvetica Neue) that's 199 `measureText` calls to lay it out once and 129 more whenever its width changes. And two things can't be had from totals at all: which letters ended up in one glyph cluster, and which glyph of a kerned pair carries the adjustment. Of 344 test paragraphs where the current, simpler Pretext matches Chrome and the revamp doesn't, those two facts decide 299.

With `getTextClusters()` in Chrome 153 behind `--enable-blink-features=ExtendedTextMetrics`, reading one table per shaped run in place of the prefixes:

- Calls per message: 199 → 30 `measureText` plus 2 `getTextClusters`. After a width change: 129 → 15.
- 10,000 messages from scratch: 2.0 s → 0.7 s when the page reuses its canvases. Laying 10,000 kept messages out again at three widths: 2.3–3.5 s → 0.6–0.8 s. (My machine was busy during these runs; over six pairs the ratios were 0.32–0.35 and 0.15–0.25.)
- The 344 paragraphs: 325 now match Chrome, with no font-specific data. 14 of the rest hold U+FFFC, which Canvas measures as a zero width space where layout gives it 1em, so that's not this API's doing.
- The positions agree with layout's when Canvas is handed layout's run: I send the whole run with `textRendering = 'optimizeLegibility'`, with U+2028 standing in for U+0020 so Canvas doesn't shape word by word, at the zoomed font size. Against Range rects, 12,987 of 13,035 cluster starts in 1,268 paragraphs floor to the DOM's value, and most of the rest are negative letter spacing, where a rect's left edge isn't the cluster's start.
- It already works on OffscreenCanvas and in workers, which is where a library like this lives.

A tiny standalone page with the prefix-against-clusters comparison, no dependencies: https://gist.github.com/chenglou/87e9a5c7b1a75ad1c3fdbee905a27976. On my machine it measures 300 words in three fonts with 4,817 `measureText` calls by prefixes against 300 + 300 calls by clusters, and shows where the two disagree (ligatures and kerned pairs, where a prefix shapes differently from the whole word).

A few thoughts from using it:

- What I'd love most is knowing whether the text can be split at a cluster's start without reshaping either side. Every `measureText` call my line breaker still makes after the change above (15 per message per width) is there to work that out, and Blink already keeps the answer per glyph right next to the position (`glyph_data.IsSafeToBreakBefore()` in `ComputePositionData`). A boolean on `TextCluster` would take a width change to zero Canvas calls; an experiment that skips those questions puts the three-width case at about 0.1 s instead of 0.6 s.
- It would help to get every cluster, including the ones with no advance (soft hyphen, ZWSP, U+2060, ZWNJ after a space), and the advance itself or `x` as a double. `x` is a float32, so past 256 px it no longer holds the exact 16.16 sum; today I ask twice with `align: 'left'` and `align: 'right'` and subtract, which is exact but costs two calls.
- A smaller one: a call builds one `TextCluster` object per cluster, so for a 110-character string `measureText` alone is 4.2 µs and the two calls together are 26 µs. A form that fills typed arrays would be several times cheaper. I'd happily take the API as it is, though.

I also ran into two implementation bugs in Chrome 153 (cluster starts wrapping past 65,535 units, and the list depending on how V8 stores the string); I've filed them on the Chromium tracker (https://issues.chromium.org/issues/564022255, https://issues.chromium.org/issues/564022256) since they aren't spec matters. Happy to share more numbers or the prototype. Thanks again!

The WebKit proposal is considerably more functional than the proposal here. I see it in the spirit of earlier Canvas Formatted Text proposals where the goal was to support HTML-like multi-line formatting to canvas text, such as https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/Canvas/FormattedText.md.

Comparing the WebKit and Chromium proposals, the Chromium proposed functionality a essentially a subset of the WebKit proposal differing in the details. In particular the WebKit proposal:

* Uses `GlyphRun` instead of `TextCluster`.
* `GlpyhRun` must have a `TextRun` which essentially has `start` and `end` from `TextCluster`
* `GlpyhRun.split` instead of `TextMetrics.getTextClusters`.
* `GlyphRun.advanceToPosition` instead of `TextMetrics.getIndexFromOffset`
* `GlyphRun.selectionRect` instead of `TextMetrics.getSelectionRects`
* `GlpyhRun.textMetrics` to get additional geometric information, instead of `TextMetrics.getActualBoundingBox`.

The baseline and align attributes are no longer needed on all the glyph runs because they are now independent from any `TextMetrics` object created with a particular align and baseline.

Assuming there is a constructor for `TextRun`, almost all of the Google proposal's functionality could be could be implemented now with very little modification for a future WebKit proposal.

I prefer the WebKit approach of defining `GlyphRun` and `TextRun`, and adding to `CanvasText` rather than `TextMetrics`. I also like the WebKit proposal to add more functionality to the JS `Intl.Segmenter` API.
